how-much-to-charge.html.text:
← Drywall bid calculator

How much should I charge for drywall?

Enough to cover the finish you will actually leave on the wall, not enough to match the cheapest postcard on the block. A basement hang-and-texture special and a Level 5 skim under a skylight are not the same job, and a flat price per square foot cannot see the difference.

Open the free bid calculator

Price the hang, then the finish

Start with length × width × height on each room. Add the ceiling when you are hanging it. Subtract openings once — doors and windows are not board. Add waste. Then price hang and finish as two different hour stacks. Gypsum Association finish levels 0–5 are a useful language for that stack: Level 0 is hang only, Level 3 is what a heavy texture can hide, Level 4 is the usual paint-ready house, and Level 5 is a full skim for critical lighting. Those are not the same week.

Height and openings are not “included”

An 8-ft closet is the hang you already priced. A 12-ft great room is not twice the hours, but it is not the same hours either — stilts, lifts, and carrying add a real fraction. Each door and window is a cut, a tape line, and a bead, not a hole that makes the job cheaper. If those lines are “included” in a $1.50-a-foot special, they are unpaid.

Texture is a second labor list

Orange peel, knockdown, and skip trowel are hours and material after the finish coats, not a free upgrade. Contractors who quote only the hang and “figure texture in” are guessing the line that most often blows a basement special. 4×12 sheets cut joint tape versus 4×8; that is visible in the takeoff, not in a blended square-foot price.

Then load the wage and keep a margin

A hanger paid $34 often costs more than $44 once employer taxes, stilts-and-tear-out workers’ compensation, liability, and paid time off are counted. Overhead sits on top of that direct cost. Margin is a share of the price the customer sees, not a markup you add last and forget. The walk-away number is total cost: below it the job makes nothing, even before you pay yourself.

This is not a Gypsum Association price list

This is not a Gypsum Association production table, not a building-code requirement, and not a finding that a wall is fire-rated, permitted, or paint-ready. The starting hours and material figures are ballpark numbers so a contractor can see the shape of a bid. Replace them with times and invoices from your own jobs, confirm measurements on site, and have a qualified professional review anything that has to be signed or insured.

Price this job in the calculator

Common questions

How much should I charge for drywall?

Charge the hours and material the job will actually take — net hung area plus waste, times hang, finish level, texture, height, openings, travel, and a dumpster if you are tearing out — then divide cost by one minus your target margin. A flat price per square foot hides the difference between a hang-and-texture basement and a Level 5 skim under critical lighting.

Why do two rooms of the same size bid so differently?

Finish level, texture, height, and openings. Hanging is the cheap half. Level 4 paint-ready is not Level 3 plus a spray, and a 12-ft ceiling is not an 8-ft closet. A neighborhood special that ignores those lines is how a crew works a week for a three-day price.

Is this a Gypsum Association price list?

No. Starting hours and material figures are editable ballpark numbers, not a Gypsum Association production table, a code specification, or a finding that any wall is fire-rated, permitted, or paint-ready. Confirm measurements on site.

No warranty. This free page is not legal, tax, financial, or engineering advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. It is not a manufacturer, building-code, fire-rating, or insurance inspection. Verify every figure against your own costs and a qualified professional before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

FOR DRYWALL CONTRACTORS

Bid the finish level, not the sheets.

Hanging is the cheap half. A basement hang-and-texture special is not the same job as a Level 5 skim under a skylight, and a flat price per square foot cannot see the difference. Price the rooms, the waste, the height, the openings, and the finish — then see the walk-away number before a $1.50-a-foot special eats the week.

How much should I charge for drywall? · This calculator vs. Buildxact · This calculator vs. a flat price per square foot

The rooms

One row per room. Length × width × height makes the walls; check ceiling when you are hanging it. Openings come off the total below — do not pre-subtract them here or you will double-count.

The job

Finish levels follow the Gypsum Association idea (0 hang-only through 5 full skim) as a time budget you can edit — not a specification, inspection, or a finding that any wall is fire-rated, permitted, or paint-ready. Waste covers cuts and damaged sheets. Height over 8 ft multiplies hang, finish, and texture hours on that room.

Your costs

Payroll burden covers employer taxes, workers’ compensation (stilts, lifts, and tear-out are not cheap), liability insurance, and paid time off. A hanger paid $34 often costs more than $44 on the wall. Underestimating that is how a $1.50-a-foot special loses money.

The starting hours and material figures are common ballpark numbers, not a Gypsum Association table, a code specification, or a guarantee — time your own crews and replace them. This is not a finding that any wall is fire-rated, permitted, or paint-ready.

    Hand the customer a proposal

    The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

    Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

    Common questions

    What does this drywall estimate include?

    Each room’s wall and optional ceiling area net of openings, a waste percentage rolled into a sheet count, hang labor by board type, finish labor by level, texture labor and material, tear-off of existing drywall when you flag it, add-ons like stilts or extra corner bead, and overhead and margin on top.

    What’s the difference between finish level 4 and finish level 5?

    Level 4 is the typical paint-ready residential job; level 5 is a full skim coat used where critical or raking light would otherwise show joint lines. The tool applies more finish hours and more mud per 100 square feet as the level goes up — these are ballpark starting hours, not a production standard.

    Does choosing Type X board mean the wall is fire-rated?

    No. Type X is priced here only as a material choice with its own waste percentage and hours. The tool does not evaluate or certify any fire rating, which depends on the full wall assembly and a building inspector’s sign-off, not on the board alone.

    Why does ceiling height matter if I’m not hanging the ceiling?

    Taller walls take longer to hang and finish even at the same square footage, so rooms over 8, 10, and 12 feet get a labor multiplier applied room by room. A 12-foot great room will not inflate the hours for an 8-foot closet in the same job.

    Is my data uploaded anywhere?

    No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. Inputs and business details are optionally saved in this browser’s local storage, and a share link encodes only the quote fields in the page’s URL hash, not sent to us.

    How is the sheet count estimated?

    Net hung area — walls plus any ceiling, minus openings — gets your waste percentage added, and that billable area is then divided by the sheet size you pick and rounded up, so the estimate is always a whole number of sheets you can actually order.

vs-a-flat-price-per-square-foot.html.text:
← Drywall Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat price per square foot

Drywall crews are shopped by the square foot. That rate cannot see the job — hanging is the cheap half, and finish level, texture, height, and openings decide whether the same footage pays, and two rooms of identical area can differ by more than three times in labor.

What a flat price per square foot is

A price per square foot is the fastest number to quote over the phone: pace off the room, multiply by a rate, read back a total. It is also the unit customers already compare between competing bids.

The rate behind it was learned from a specific job — a given finish level, texture, and ceiling height — and then reused for the next square footage that calls in, whether or not that next job shares any of those.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter each room's length, width, and height, openings, waste, board type, finish level, texture, and whether you are tearing out existing board, plus your own wage, payroll burden, travel, dumpster, overhead, and target margin. It nets wall and ceiling area against openings, applies a height multiplier room by room, and prices hang, finish, and texture hours separately — for this job, not a rate carried over from the last one.

What a flat per-square-foot rate doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same rate for a hang-only wall and a full Level 5 skim of the identical area, even though finish level is where most of the labor lives. Prices hang and finish hours separately by Gypsum Association finish level 0–5, so a critical-lighting skim costs more without anyone eyeballing a surcharge.
Has no line for texture — a smooth ceiling and a heavy knockdown get the same rate, even though texture is its own labor and material. Prices texture hours and material as their own line on top of the base hang and finish hours.
Has no line for ceiling height — an 8-ft closet and a 12-ft great room of the same footage get the same rate. Applies a height multiplier room by room, so a taller room costs more without inflating the rest of the job.
Bills openings inside the same blended per-foot number, if at all. Nets opening square footage out of billable wall area and prices opening labor and tape separately.
Gives the crew a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the price per square foot and the walk-away price alongside the total, so a shopped rate can be scored against real cost before you match it.

Same 1,954 square feet, two different jobs

Using this calculator's own shipped cost inputs — $34 hourly wage, 32% burden, a 1/2" regular board, 10% waste, 86 sq ft of openings across 7 openings, $75 trip fee, 16% overhead, 26% target margin:

A 1,954 sq ft hang-and-finish job at Level 1 (fire-tape, joints covered) takes 46.4 hours and prices at $5,473.07 for the job — $2.80 per square foot.

Finish the identical 1,954 sq ft to Level 5 instead — a full skim for critical lighting, same rooms, same waste, same openings — and it takes 152.8 hours, costs $10,536.55 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices it at $14,238.58 — $7.29 per square foot. Quoting the Level 5 job at the Level 1 job's learned rate of $2.80 per square foot reproduces the Level 1 price, $5,473.07, which is $5,063.48 below the Level 5 job's own break-even cost — before counting the $8,765.51 it falls short of this calculator's own price at a 26% target margin. Same square footage, same rate, one job that pays and one that loses money the moment the mud goes on.

Common questions

Why does a flat price per square foot get a drywall bid wrong?

Because square footage only measures the area, not what it takes to finish it. A 1,954 sq ft hang-and-finish job at Level 1 (fire-tape, joints covered) takes about 46.4 hours. The identical 1,954 sq ft finished to Level 5 (a full skim for critical lighting) takes about 152.8 hours -- more than three times the labor on the same area, because hanging is the cheap half and finish level is where the hours actually go.

What does a flat per-square-foot rate usually miss entirely?

Finish level, texture, ceiling height, and openings. A flat rate has no line for the difference between a hang-only wall and a full Level 5 skim, no line for a textured ceiling versus a smooth one, no line for a 12-ft great room taking longer per foot than an 8-ft closet, and no line for a room dense with doors and windows netting out less billable board than an open wall of the same footage.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

Using this calculator's own shipped cost inputs on a 1,954 sq ft hang-and-finish job: Level 1 (fire-tape) takes 46.4 hours and prices at $5,473.07 for the job -- $2.80 per square foot. The identical 1,954 sq ft finished to Level 5 (full skim) takes 152.8 hours, costs $10,536.55 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices it at $14,238.58 -- $7.29 per square foot. Quoting the Level 5 job at the Level 1 job's learned rate of $2.80 per square foot reproduces the Level 1 price, $5,473.07, which is $5,063.48 below the Level 5 job's own break-even cost -- before counting the $8,765.51 it falls short of this calculator's price at a 26% target margin.

Is a flat price per square foot ever a reasonable shorthand?

For a narrow band of similar jobs -- the same finish level, texture, and ceiling height as the job the rate was learned on -- a per-foot number can land close. The risk is quoting a Level 5 skim, a textured ceiling, or a run of 12-ft walls the same way sight unseen, because the rate does not know the finish level, the texture, or the height until the crew is on site, and by then the per-foot number has often already been quoted.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or material costs?

No. It has no data on your local labor market or your supplier's board and mud pricing. It takes each room's dimensions, finish level, texture, and openings, and your own wage, payroll burden, board and tape material, waste, travel, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into hang and finish hours and a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat per-square-foot rate skips, not a market survey.

Verify every figure against your own payroll, insurance, material, and dumpster costs before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device, and this page makes no live comparison against any competing service — it is a static page describing the calculator's own worked example.

vs-buildxact.html.text:
← Drywall Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. Buildxact

Two different shapes: Buildxact is account-based estimating and project-management software for running a construction business across trades and jobs. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this hang-and-finish job cost, given its rooms and finish level, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

Buildxact is construction estimating and project-management software founded in Australia in 2011, with North American headquarters in Austin, Texas. It serves builders, remodelers, and contractors across trades — including carpentry, painting, roofing, and flooring — combining material takeoffs, quoting, job costing, scheduling, and client communication into one subscription system meant to run a whole business across every job and every trade on the crew. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account. Buildxact's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — multi-trade construction estimating and project-management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Buildxact appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Buildxact does. It does not manage takeoffs across trades, schedule crews, track job costs over time, or store any project record on a server. It takes one drywall job's rooms — each with wall and optional ceiling area net of openings — a waste percentage, a ceiling-height labor multiplier, Gypsum Association finish levels 0-5, texture, tear-out of existing board, add-ons, and the drive, plus loaded wage, dumpster, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the price per hung square foot, the sheet count, the labor-hour split between hang and finish, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a price on the table, a check of whether it clears that walk-away floor. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.
